strengths: The core observation is well-motivated and clearly articulated: output length is inherently stochastic because termination is determined by sampling an EOS token, so point estimates clash with the decoding process. Figure 1 and the empirical statistics (skewness, CV, quantile ratios) support this convincingly.

The paper provides both empirical and theoretical grounding for the heavy-tailed modeling choice: Theorem 3.2 derives power-law tail decay under a mixture assumption on termination rates, with a complete proof in Appendix A, and Table 1 systematically compares candidate distribution families with KS tests.

The proposed TIE metric is technically clean: censored expectation and CVaR for the log-t distribution are derived correctly (Appendix B), the censoring at max_tokens neatly handles the infinite-mean problem of the log-t distribution, and the adaptive risk coefficient β plus waiting-time decay address system pressure and starvation.

Evaluation is unusually comprehensive: two main Llama models plus six additional model families (including MoE) and an industry-grade model, three datasets, both online and offline scenarios, ablations over distribution family, score computation, sample size, and degrees of freedom, plus an implementation with asynchronous batched prediction on vLLM and measured scheduling overhead.
Limitations are honestly discussed (Appendix E): training data collection requires repeated generations per prompt, and the authors acknowledge this prevents direct use of online serving data.
weaknesses: The theoretical link between the model and the fitted distribution is loose: Theorem 3.2 yields a power-law exponent α that is prompt- and workload-dependent, but the method fixes ν = 3.5 globally based on empirical KS fits. The paper never reconciles the theoretical exponent with the fixed tail parameter, weakening the claim that the theory 'proves' the log-t fit.

Assumption A.2 (a fixed per-trajectory termination rate p̃ determined at generation start) is a strong idealization that is asserted rather than validated; the proof essentially shows heavy tails follow from assuming a heavy-tailed mixture, so the theoretical contribution is more of a consistency argument than an independent justification.

Baselines are limited to non-preemptive methods (FCFS, SSJF, LTR). The related work argues preemptive/iterative methods (TRAIL, ELIS) incur high overhead, but no direct empirical comparison is provided, so the claim that distributional prediction is the better way to handle uncertainty is not fully tested. Relatedly, Chen et al. (2025b) on robust inference optimization under prediction uncertainty appears closely related but is neither compared against nor discussed in depth.

No statistical rigor around reported results: no confidence intervals, error bars, or repeated-run variance, which matters given the heavy-tailed workloads studied; improvements of e.g., 1.42× could be sensitive to run-to-run variance.

The sensitivity of the score to the censoring point is unexplored: E[X̃] includes a term xmax · P(X > xmax), so results may depend heavily on the max_tokens configuration, yet no ablation over max_tokens is reported.

Training data collection is expensive (20 repeated generations per prompt) and, while the paper argues total data scale is matched across methods, the compute cost asymmetry versus 900K single-generation samples for baselines is not quantified. Fairness for long requests is addressed only via a decay heuristic, with no quantitative fairness metrics (e.g., tail waiting times of long jobs) reported.

strengths: The core observation that per-prompt output length varies across repeated generations (Figure 1, Table 1) is empirically well-supported, and the systematic comparison of distribution families via KS pass rates is a useful analysis.

The scheduling system is thoughtfully engineered: asynchronous prediction with dynamic batching, min-heap queue, starvation-prevention decay, and censored CVaR computation (Appendix B) show real systems maturity.

Evaluation breadth is good: online chatbot and offline SDG scenarios, three datasets, 8B/70B Llama models plus six additional model families including MoE (Tables 5-6), with ablations on distribution family, score computation, and sample size.
The generalization experiments (predictors trained only on LMSYS/Llama-8B data, tested on ShareGPT, Alpaca, and other models) are a meaningful test that many scheduling papers skip.
The limitations section (Appendix E) honestly acknowledges the costly multi-generation training data requirement.
weaknesses: The central conceptual claim is overstated. The paper argues that point estimates 'do not match the stochastic decoding process,' but a point estimate of the conditional mean is perfectly well-defined under stochastic decoding (and is exactly what SEPT theory prescribes). The real issue is prediction error, not a conceptual mismatch. Moreover, the paper never states the decoding temperature used in its serving experiments; under greedy/temperature-0 serving (common in production), output length per prompt is deterministic and the motivating argument largely collapses.

Theorem 3.2 is close to circular: Assumption 3.1 (termination-rate density behaves as c·p^(α-1) near zero) directly presupposes the heavy-tailed mixture structure it is used to derive. The empirical motivation for this specific density shape is thin, and a power-law tail (Theorem 3.2) does not actually imply the log-t family — the choice of log-t remains purely empirical, with ν=3.5 tuned on the same data used for evaluation.

KS p-values are computed with parameters estimated by MLE on the same samples, which invalidates standard KS critical values; the reported pass rates are therefore not statistically rigorous without a parametric bootstrap.

The headline gains overstate the novelty's contribution. Table 4 shows SEPT (E[X] alone) already achieves 0.75 vs. TIE's 0.67 s/token; most of the benefit comes from distributional prediction, and the CVaR/risk-adaptive component (the actual 'TIE' idea) contributes modestly and is sensitive to hand-tuned hyperparameters (α=0.9, β in [0.1,0.5], γ=0.9, τ=30s) chosen without justification.

No preemptive baselines are compared (TRAIL, ELIS, S3 are cited as SOTA in Section 1 but excluded), so the claim of improvement over 'the best-performing baseline' is restricted to a narrow non-preemptive comparison that the authors themselves identify as a limited class.

Fairness and starvation are discussed as motivation for the waiting-time decay, but no fairness metrics are reported (e.g., tail waiting time or completion time of long requests). P90 per-token latency improvements could come at the expense of systematically delayed long requests, and this trade-off is invisible in the evaluation.

The training data requirement is substantial and asymmetric: 45K prompts × 20 generations each is ~900K generations for TIE vs. 900K single generations for baselines — the 'consistent training data scale' framing obscures that TIE's data collection is far more expensive per unit of prompt coverage, which also limits the predictor's semantic diversity.

Reproducibility is undermined: the paper references 'our code' and 'details available in our code' but provides no repository link, and several critical details (decoding temperature, max_tokens used for censoring in each experiment, exact β schedule) are unspecified.

Minor presentation issues: 'e measure the system pressure' (Sec. 5, p.5), inconsistent generation counts (100 in Sec. 3.1 vs. 256 in Figure 1), and the abstract's 'reduces latency by 2.31×' phrasing conflates ratio conventions.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem (LLM inference scheduling) with a clean, well-motivated idea: modeling output length as a distribution rather than a point estimate, which is a genuinely sensible framing given stochastic decoding.
The distribution-fitting study is reasonably thorough: multiple heavy-tailed families are compared (Table 1), the log-t choice is justified with KS tests, and the fixed ν=3.5 variant is ablated.

The theoretical analysis (Theorem 3.2, Appendix A) is a nice touch, connecting mixture-of-geometric termination rates to power-law tail decay, and it correctly explains the empirical heavy-tail behavior.

The evaluation is broad: online chatbot and offline SDG scenarios, three datasets, 8B/70B Llama models plus six additional models (including MoE architectures and DeepSeek-R1-distill) in Appendices D and F, generalization tests, scheduling-overhead measurement, and component ablations (Table 4) that isolate the contribution of CVaR and the adaptive β.

The systems work is credible: asynchronous batched prediction on vLLM, min-heap queue with lazy score updates, starvation-prevention decay, and reported scheduling overhead (4.26 ms per request) that contextualizes the gains.
Limitations are discussed honestly (Appendix E acknowledges the costly repeated-generation requirement for training data).
weaknesses: The central argument that point estimates 'do not match' stochastic decoding is somewhat overstated. SJF only needs an ordering of realized job lengths; LTR (Fu et al., 2024) already argued exactly this. The paper never demonstrates a clear head-to-head advantage over ranking-based approaches under controlled conditions beyond the reported end-to-end numbers, and the comparison to preemptive/iterative methods (TRAIL, ELIS, S3) is only qualitative — none of them are evaluated empirically, despite being the motivation for avoiding re-prediction overhead.

There is an unresolved statistical tension: the paper itself notes the uncensored expectation of the log-t distribution does not exist (Appendix B), yet TIE's score is built on E[X] plus a CVaR term. The fitted parameters (especially σ, which shows ~20% relative error at the chosen 20 repetitions per Figure 7) strongly influence tail quantities; the sensitivity of the scheduler to σ estimation error is not analyzed, and the Monte Carlo estimation (10k samples) of tail expectations for a very heavy-tailed distribution is not validated for variance/accuracy.

The KS goodness-of-fit methodology is questionable: fitting via MLE and testing on the same data is known to inflate p-values, and the paper relies on a single KS test in Figure 1 (256 generations) while Table 1 reports 100 generations — an inconsistency in sample sizes.

The theoretical model rests on a strong assumption (a fixed effective termination rate per trajectory, density behaving as p^(α−1) near 0) whose α is never estimated or validated against data; the result itself (power-law tails from a mixture of geometrics) is a classical observation, so the theory is more explanatory than novel.

Missing fairness/starvation evaluation: a waiting-time decay mechanism is introduced precisely to prevent starvation of long requests, but no fairness metrics (e.g., tail waiting time of mispredicted/long requests) are reported, so the cost of the risk-averse policy on long requests is invisible.

Baseline training-data accounting deserves more scrutiny: SSJF/LTR use 900K distinct samples while TIE uses 45K prompts × 20 generations. Total tokens may be comparable, but the variance-reduction benefit from repeated generation of the same prompts is a fundamentally different (and cheaper-to-collect-but-rarely-available) signal; the paper acknowledges this limitation but does not quantify how TIE performs when repeated generations are unavailable.

Reproducibility is only partial: hyperparameters are listed, but key implementation details are deferred to 'our code' without a stated release, and it is unclear whether predictors were retrained per serving model in the cross-model experiments.
Several hyperparameters (α=0.9, β∈[0.1,0.5], γ=0.9, τ=30s, 3ms batching timeout) are tuned ad hoc; the adaptive β formula is heuristic without justification.

Minor presentation issues: typos ('e measure the system pressure', 'Avg. TTFT' vs. 'TTFT (s)'), and Figure 5's heatmap interpretation would benefit from quantitative clustering metrics rather than visual claims.

strengths: The core insight — that output length is inherently stochastic and should be modeled as a distribution rather than a point estimate — is well-motivated by both empirical evidence (1K prompts × 100 generations, skewness/CV/quantile-ratio statistics, per-category diagnostics in Appendix D.4) and a theoretical analysis (Theorem 3.2 with a clean, correct dominated-convergence proof in Appendix A linking a heavy-tailed termination-rate mixture to power-law tail decay).

The proposed TIE metric is simple, well-derived (censored expectation and CVaR for the log-t distribution in Appendix B, correctly handling the fact that uncensored log-t moments do not exist), and easy to deploy as a drop-in replacement in SJF scheduling on vLLM.

The empirical evaluation is unusually comprehensive: three datasets (LMSYS-Chat-1M, ShareGPT, Alpaca), nine models (including MoE architectures), online chatbot and offline SDG scenarios, three non-preemptive baselines (FCFS, SSJF, LTR) plus a preemptive baseline (TRAIL in D.8), and careful training-data-scale fairness controls (900K generations for all methods).

Thorough ablations validate each design choice: distribution family (Table 4), score computation (SEPT vs. fixed/adaptive β), sensitivity to training data scale (Table 8), sampling temperature (Table 9), fixed ν (Figure 8), and robustness to σ prediction noise (Table 12), addressing the natural concern that distributional prediction could be brittle.

The asynchronous prediction + dynamic batching implementation and the O(log n) heap-based scheduler address practical deployment concerns, and the overhead analysis (4.26 ms scheduling latency vs. multi-second TTFT) supports the claim of negligible overhead.

The limitations section is honest about the training-data requirement (multiple generations per prompt), and the learning-augmented algorithms discussion in Section 7 gives a principled framing of the consistency/robustness trade-off.
weaknesses: The central theoretical assumption (Assumption 3.1/A.2 — that each trajectory has a fixed termination rate p~ drawn from a distribution with f(p) ~ c·p^(α−1)) is asserted but not quantitatively validated against the empirical data; while the qualitative motivation (structured outputs, long-form commitments) is plausible, the paper does not measure the empirical density of termination rates or estimate α, leaving the theorem as a plausibility argument rather than a verified model.

The improvement over TRAIL is mixed: TRAIL is actually better at low load (10–40 RPS in Table 11), and TIE's advantage emerges only at moderate/high load where preemption costs dominate; the main text's framing could be more balanced about this regime dependence.

Some aspects of the model conflates sources of variance: the fitted log-t per prompt captures stochastic decoding variation under one temperature (0.7), but real serving systems vary temperature/top-p; the temperature sensitivity study (Table 9) partially mitigates this but a distribution fitted at one temperature is only heuristically transferred to others.

The choice of hyperparameters (α=0.9, β ∈ [0.1, 0.5] with the specific adaptive form in Eq. 12, γ=0.9, τ=30s, 3ms prediction batching timeout) is largely empirical; while ablations support the adaptive β, the sensitivity of the full system to other settings is less thoroughly explored.

KS-test-based goodness-of-fit at 100 samples per prompt has low power to reject fits; the 90–93% pass-rate comparison across distribution families could be less discriminative than presented, and the end-to-end gap (Table 4) is the more meaningful evidence.

The theoretical contribution is modest — the result is a standard heavy-tail characterization conditional on an untested assumption — so the paper's main value is empirical/systems-oriented, which fits ICML only at the interface of learning-augmented scheduling rather than as core ML theory.

strengths: The paper targets a practically important problem (queue-level HOL blocking in LLM serving) and the proposed scheduler is simple, implementable on vLLM, and evaluated with unusual breadth: 3 datasets, 9 models including MoE architectures, online and offline scenarios, ablations of the distribution family and score function (Table 4), sensitivity to training scale, temperature, and adaptive vs. fixed beta (Appendix D).

The empirical observation that per-prompt output length distributions are heavy-tailed (Skewness ~3.1, P99/P50 ~10.77, Table 7 breakdown by prompt family) is interesting and potentially useful beyond scheduling.

The asynchronous prediction and dynamic batching design (Section 5) is a sensible systems contribution, and the overhead analysis (4.26 ms per request vs. ~48 s TTFT) supports the claim that prediction cost is negligible.

The comparison with a preemptive scheduler (TRAIL, Table 11) and the robustness analysis to sigma prediction noise (Table 12) address obvious objections and are commendable. The limitations section is honest about the multi-generation training data requirement.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claim is largely circular. Theorem 3.2 'proves' heavy-tailed output lengths from Assumption 3.1, which directly assumes a power-law density near p=0; the heavy-tailed conclusion is essentially baked into the premise. The proof (Appendix A) is a standard dominated-convergence argument, and the framing as 'some mild assumptions' (Section 1) oversells a result whose content is the assumption itself, not a property of LLM decoding.

The goodness-of-fit methodology is weak evidence for the log-t distribution. The KS test is applied with only ~100 samples per prompt, where it has very low power and fails to reject many candidate distributions; a 90-93% 'pass rate' at p>0.05 does not establish that log-t is the correct family, especially given the choice nu=3.5 was itself tuned on this data (Appendix D.3), which invalidates nominal p-values.

The headline attribution is questionable: the ablation (Table 4) shows plain SEPT with the same predictor achieves 0.75 s/token vs. TIE's 0.67 (~11% gain), meaning most of the reported 2.31x improvement over LTR comes from ordinary SJF scheduling plus distributional prediction, not from the uncertainty/tail-risk mechanism that constitutes the paper's claimed novelty. The uncertainty-aware component, which the paper's narrative centers on, contributes a modest marginal gain.

The motivation that point estimates 'do not match the stochastic decoding process' is overstated. Output length is stochastic only under sampling; the claim's practical relevance depends on deployment sampling configurations, and the paper's own temperature sweep (Table 9) shows the effect varies substantially. No argument is given for why a well-calibrated point predictor could not match TIE's ranking quality without distributional machinery.

Fairness and starvation behavior is under-evaluated. SJF-style policies can severely delay long requests; the waiting-time decay is introduced with default parameters (gamma=0.9, tau=30s) but no tail-latency distribution for long requests (e.g., worst-case JCT, or JCT conditioned on output length) is reported, so the cost TIE imposes on long requests remains unquantified.

The training data requirement (45K prompts x 20 generations = 900K generations) is presented as 'equal data scale' to baselines, but repeated generation per prompt is a materially different and more constrained collection process; the paper itself concedes production logs cannot be used directly, which limits real-world applicability.

The significance of the 'connection to learning-augmented algorithms' (Section 7) is asserted rather than demonstrated: no consistency/robustness guarantees or competitive bounds are derived; the discussion is a conceptual analogy only.

strengths: The central observation that output lengths of LLM requests are inherently stochastic (determined by when EOS is sampled) rather than fixed quantities is well-motivated and leads to a natural reframing: fit a distribution per request rather than a point estimate. This is a genuinely useful conceptual contribution to LLM scheduling.

The empirical characterization is careful: 1K prompts × 100 generations from LMSYS-Chat-1M, with skewness/CV/quantile-ratio statistics and a per-prompt-family breakdown (Appendix D.4) showing heavy-tailed behavior is not an artifact of specific prompt types.

Theorem 3.2 (power-law tail decay under Assumption 3.1) with a complete proof in Appendix A provides theoretical grounding for why heavy tails should arise from the decoding process, connecting to the broader heavy-tail literature.

The risk-sensitive score E[X̃] + β·CVaR is simple, well-derived (censored log-t expectation and CVaR derived cleanly in Appendix B, including the necessary censoring since uncensored log-t moments do not exist), and the adaptive β connects nicely to the consistency/robustness framing of learning-augmented algorithms.

Experiments are unusually thorough: online chatbot and offline SDG scenarios, 2 headline models plus 7 additional models (including MoE), 3 datasets, cross-model/cross-dataset generalization, ablations over distribution family and score computation (Table 4 shows the log-t fit matters, not just CVaR: log-normal 1.63 vs log-t 0.67 s/token), sensitivity to training scale, temperature, σ-noise robustness, and a comparison against a preemptive baseline (TRAIL).

The systems contributions (asynchronous batched prediction, min-heap with lazy priority updates) are practical, and the overhead analysis (4.26 ms/request vs 48.23 s TTFT) supports the claim that the approach is deployable.
Limitations are honestly discussed (multi-generation training data requirement) with quantified sensitivity analysis (Appendix D.5), and future work is well-scoped.
weaknesses: The theoretical result is somewhat circular: Theorem 3.2's heavy-tailedness follows directly from Assumption 3.1 (f(p) ~ c·p^{α-1} near zero), which is asserted rather than validated empirically. The paper proves a consequence of the assumption but does not test whether the termination-rate distribution actually satisfies it, so the theorem is best read as a plausibility argument rather than evidence.

There is tension in the framing: a substantial fraction of output-length variance across requests comes from prompt content rather than decoding randomness, and greedy decoding is deterministic. The paper fixes temperature=0.7 throughout main experiments; Appendix D.6 shows degradation at other temperatures, but the 'inherent stochasticity' narrative could be more carefully scoped (e.g., how much of the tail is attributable to sampling vs. prompt ambiguity).

The high KS p-values are treated as strong evidence of fit, but KS has low power at these sample sizes and high p-values do not confirm a distribution; the log-t conclusion would be better supported by out-of-sample quantile calibration or tail-specific metrics.

Potential baseline-fairness concern: TIE is trained on 45K prompts × 20 repeated generations while SSJF/LTR see 900K single generations. Although generation counts are equalized, TIE's training signal contains per-prompt distributional information that point-estimate baselines structurally cannot access; a fairer comparison would include a point-estimate predictor trained on the same repeated-generation data (e.g., predicting the mean over 20 runs).

The comparison with TRAIL (Appendix D.8) shows TIE loses at low load (≤40 RPS), yet the headline abstract claims (2.31× latency reduction, 1.42× throughput) are quoted without load qualification; the strongest gains occur only at high load.

Several scheduler hyperparameters (γ=0.9, τ=30s, α=0.9, β range [0.1, 0.5]) are set without ablation; the adaptive β formula (Eq. 12) appears hand-tuned, and the range of possible starvation/fairness outcomes under the decay mechanism is not characterized beyond the existence of the mechanism.

Reproducibility relies on 'Details are available in our code' without an explicit anonymized artifact link, and Monte Carlo scoring (10k samples per request) cost under high load is only briefly analyzed.
The paper does not discuss interaction with other serving knobs (chunked prefill, disaggregated prefill/decode), so the claimed TTFT gains may shift under more modern serving configurations.
